explanations.answer: It will all be made known
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, "For there is nothing concealed that will not be disclosed, and nothing hidden that will not be made known." That's the reason He gives right after telling them not to be afraid of the people against them. Baker, I once hid a burnt batch behind the flour canister. The smell had the whole bakery knowing in about four minutes.

explanations.answer: It will stay hidden for good
explanations.explanation: Jesus says the opposite. He says there is "…nothing hidden that will not be made known." This comes right after "So do not be afraid of them." Nothing concealed stays that way, baker, and I've learned that about crumbs on my apron too.

Jesus never says anything about fading. He says nothing concealed "…will not be disclosed…" That's a coming out into the open, not a slipping away. Memory fading is my department, baker, because I forget what my own timer is for twice a day.

Jesus says the opposite. He tells them, "What I tell you in the dark, speak in the daylight; what is whispered in your ear, proclaim from the housetops." The whisper is meant to go out. Baker, a secret with a megaphone attached is not much of a secret.

Right, baker. Jesus says, "What I tell you in the dark, speak in the daylight; what is whispered in your ear, proclaim from the housetops." So what's whispered in their ears is meant to be spoken out loud. I think that's the biggest volume change I've ever heard of, from a whisper straight to a rooftop.

Jesus says, "Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul." This is a heavy line, baker, so I'll say it plainly. The ones He's talking about can kill the body, and the soul is the part they cannot kill. I'm glad it's right there in black and white.

The verses just before tell the disciples to speak in the daylight and proclaim from the housetops. But Jesus says, "Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul." It's a heavy line, so I'll leave it there. The soul is the answer.

Family does come up later in this passage, in the verses about a man's own household. Here, though, Jesus says, "Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul." It's a heavy line, baker, so I'll say it plainly. The word is soul.

explanations.answer: The One who can destroy soul and body
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, "Instead, fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell." It's a serious line, so I'll let it be serious. Notice who He just told them not to fear, the ones who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Now He points them to the One with the real weight.

explanations.answer: The governors who judge them in court
explanations.explanation: Earlier Jesus does warn that they'll be brought before governors and kings (Matthew 10:18). But in this passage He points somewhere else for fear. He says, "Instead, fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell." This is a heavy one, baker, so I'll say it plainly and move along.

explanations.answer: The councils that hand them over
explanations.explanation: Earlier Jesus does say they'll be handed over to local councils (Matthew 10:17). But here He tells them, "Instead, fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell." It's a heavy line, baker, so no jokes from me on this one. The councils aren't who He points to.

Jesus says, "Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from the will of your Father." Those are two sparrows sold for a penny, baker. And still the Father's will is in the picture for every one. I think that's the whole point of the comparison.

This one is true, baker. Jesus says, "Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from the will of your Father." He says it about birds that sell two for a penny. If the Father's will reaches even there, I'd say that's worth hearing twice.
Jesus says, "So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows." He says it right after the sparrows and the numbered hairs. Baker, not just more than one sparrow, but MORE than many.

explanations.answer: About the same as two sparrows
explanations.explanation: Jesus sets the bar much higher. He says, "you are worth more than many sparrows." Two sparrows is just the penny price He mentions two verses earlier. Many sparrows is a lot more than two, and you're worth more than that.
It's the other direction, baker. Jesus says, "you are worth more than many sparrows." Not less than one, but more than many. He begins that verse with "So do not be afraid…" and I think this is why.

Jesus says it the other way. He promises, "Therefore everyone who confesses Me before men, I will also confess him before My Father in heaven." Then He says, "But whoever denies Me before men, I will also deny him before My Father in heaven." It's a serious pair of lines, baker, so I'll keep it straight.

That's right. Jesus says, "But whoever denies Me before men, I will also deny him before My Father in heaven." It sits right beside the promise about those who confess Him. It's a serious line, baker, so I'll let it stand on its own.

Jesus says, "Do not assume that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword." The next verses show what He means, baker, a man against his father, a daughter against her mother. I'd say that's one to read slowly.

A crown would've been easier to hear, baker, and I only have room on my head for the one tall hat anyway. But Jesus says, "I have not come to bring peace, but a sword." The next verses name the division He's talking about, a man turned against his father and a daughter against her mother.

A scroll would've been a quiet one, baker. But Jesus says, "I have not come to bring peace, but a sword." He starts by saying "Do not assume…" so He's heading off the wrong guess. Then He explains with the household lines in the verses after.

Jesus says the opposite. He says, "Anyone who loves his father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me; anyone who loves his son or daughter more than Me is not worthy of Me…" I think that one stings for a dad like me, baker. But it's what He says.

Right, baker. Jesus says, "Anyone who loves his father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me; anyone who loves his son or daughter more than Me is not worthy of Me…" He says it about both directions in a family. I think it's a hard one to hear, and He says it plainly.

Jesus says, "…anyone who does not take up his cross and follow Me is not worthy of Me." A follower takes up a cross and follows. Baker, I carry a rolling pin on a normal day. Jesus is talking about something far heavier.

Earlier Jesus actually tells the disciples to take no staff for the journey (Matthew 10:10). Here He says, "…anyone who does not take up his cross and follow Me is not worthy of Me." The thing to take up is a cross, not a staff, baker.

A lamp is a handy thing in a dark bakery, baker, I'll give you that. But Jesus says, "…anyone who does not take up his cross and follow Me is not worthy of Me." The word in the verse is cross. Nothing about a lamp here.

Jesus says, "…whoever loses his life for My sake will find it." It's the other half of the line about finding your life and losing it. The turn is what makes it land. Lose it for His sake and you find it.
Jesus doesn't say waste. He says, "…whoever loses his life for My sake will find it." Losing it for His sake ends in finding, baker, not waste.
Regret is what I feel after cookie number four, baker. But Jesus says, "…whoever loses his life for My sake will find it." Nothing about regret in the line. The word is find.

explanations.answer: Jesus and the One who sent Him
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, "He who receives you receives Me, and he who receives Me receives the One who sent Me." That's two steps in one sentence, baker. Receive the disciples and you're receiving Jesus. Receive Jesus and you're receiving the One who sent Him.

Prophets come up in the very next verse, but not as the answer to this one. Here Jesus says, "He who receives you receives Me, and he who receives Me receives the One who sent Me." So it's Jesus, and then the One who sent Him. The prophets get their own line right after.

Jesus doesn't mention angels anywhere in this verse. He says, "He who receives you receives Me, and he who receives Me receives the One who sent Me." It goes from the disciples to Jesus to the One who sent Him. That's a short chain, and it's a big one.

Jesus says, "Whoever receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward…" Receiving a prophet because he is a prophet comes with a prophet's reward. Baker, I think that's a generous deal. He says the same about receiving a righteous man because he is a righteous man.

It's true, baker. Jesus says, "Whoever receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward…" He gives the same promise for receiving a righteous man because he is a righteous man. So receiving them comes with a reward.

Jesus says, "…truly I tell you, he will never lose his reward." That's for a cup of cold water, baker, given to one of these little ones because he is His disciple. I lose my spatula every week, and Jesus says this reward isn't lost. That's a lot of comfort for something so small.

Friends are great, baker, but they're not what Jesus names. He says, "…truly I tell you, he will never lose his reward." That's for giving even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones because he is His disciple. The word is reward.

Home is a good thing to keep, baker. But Jesus says, "…truly I tell you, he will never lose his reward." He says it about anyone who gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones because he is His disciple. The word is reward.

explanations.answer: Teaches and preaches in their cities
explanations.explanation: Matthew 11:1 says, "After Jesus had finished instructing His twelve disciples, He went on from there to teach and preach in their cities." Baker, the instructing is done and Jesus gets right to work. I think the best way to follow a good lesson is to keep going, and He does.

explanations.answer: Rests for a while in Capernaum
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't mention rest or Capernaum. It says, "After Jesus had finished instructing His twelve disciples, He went on from there to teach and preach in their cities." So He keeps teaching and preaching. Baker, I take a break after one batch, and Jesus doesn't in this verse.

explanations.answer: Goes up a mountain alone to pray
explanations.explanation: A mountain, baker? I read that verse looking for one, and nope. Matthew 11:1 says, "After Jesus had finished instructing His twelve disciples, He went on from there to teach and preach in their cities." Teaching and preaching in their cities is what He does next.
